Today's editorials and columns examine US restrictions on Indian IT firms, India's public transport gaps, the Tata Sons leadership dispute, municipal governance under PRAGATI-50 and a book on Bastar

Bombay House, the headquarters of the Tata group

Tanmaya Nanda New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 15 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTHello and welcome to Best of Business Standard Opinion, our wrap of the day's editorial page.  The United States' suspension of eight technology companies, including Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL Tech, from the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme threatens a pathway to green cards for skilled foreign workers. While Indian IT majors expect limited immediate impact, the move could raise hiring and compliance costs over time. Nasscom notes that firms have reduced H-1B dependence and increased local US hiring, with registrations by six leading Indian IT firms falling 92 per cent in financial year 2027. Today's first editorial warns that the restrictions, compounded by disparaging remarks from US officials, undermine the shared ambitions of the two countries.  The first all-India household travel survey by the National Statistics Office exposes India’s inadequate public transport and inequitable urban development. Only 15 per cent of workers use public transport, while 46 per cent rely on two-wheelers or cars. Commuting costs average Rs 785 monthly, rising to Rs 1,044 for urban workers, squeezing household incomes. The second editorial argues that poor transport networks and unaffordable housing force workers into unhealthy settlements far from employment centres. Greater investment in safe, extensive public transport and low-cost housing could widen employment opportunities, particularly for women. Better public transport would also ease congestion and pollution. The survey’s findings must translate into actionable policy. The leadership dispute at Tata Sons reflects a breakdown in governance, with differences among Tata Trusts trustees spilling into the holding company’s board. Laveesh Bhandari examines how the group’s tradition of absorbing professional managers into its wider family ecosystem can blur accountability and weaken the chain of command. With Air India still loss-making, Tata Digital seeking direction, Tata Electronics making major bets and artificial intelligence challenging TCS, the group needs decisive leadership. Bhandari rejects a split or compromise arrangement, arguing that the professional heading Tata Sons must have strategic autonomy, clear accountability and the confidence of Tata Trusts, while remaining at arm’s length from its ownership. PRAGATI-50, launched on September 29, seeks to sustain visible cleanliness across 50 cities, building on Swachh Bharat Mission’s gains in waste processing and collection. Amit Kapoor argues that lasting progress depends less on campaigns and targets than on municipal capacity. Audits reveal staff shortages, limited recruitment powers, weak revenues and fragmented control over urban services. New waste-management rules also risk burdening households without ensuring cities have adequate infrastructure, while waste pickers could be displaced by mechanisation. Kapoor calls for stronger municipal finances, clearer accountability, professional staffing and regional facilities, with monitoring that measures institutional capacity alongside visible outcomes. Larger cities should mentor smaller towns. Shantanu Nandan Sharma’s Rebel Bastar: History, Maoism and the search for answers in India’s Heartland draws on extensive field reporting, archival records and colonial accounts to illuminate the history, politics and tribal culture of a region that remains poorly understood. Aditi Phadnis praises its account of Bastar’s dynasties, British exploitation, the Bhumkal uprising and the enduring legacy of tribal hero Gunda Dhur. The book’s strongest section explores how Maoism took root among Bastar’s communities, shaped by their distinctive beliefs and social fabric, which the author calls the Mahua ideology. Phadnis finds the lengthy detour into Mao’s history unnecessary but considers the book outstanding for its research, despite structural weaknesses.

From the IMF's global growth forecast and Navi Pillay's Nobel Peace Prize to India's climate needs, rising healthcare costs and the debate over welfare, today's opinions examine multiple challenges

Despite warnings of a meltdown, Trump’s policies have barely dented global growth forecasts. (Illustration: Ajaya Mohanty)

Tanmaya Nanda New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 14 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTHello and welcome to Best of Business Standard Opinion, our wrap of the day's editorial page.  The IMF’s October World Economic Outlook projects global growth at 3.1 per cent in 2026 and 3.4 per cent in 2027, while raising India’s growth forecast for the current year to 7 per cent on resilient domestic demand. Today's first editorial highlights how energy supply rerouting, inventory drawdowns, renewables and investment in artificial intelligence have helped the world economy withstand recent shocks. However, these buffers have limits, and disappointing AI returns could unsettle financial markets. Growth is also concentrating in fewer countries, heightening risks amid elevated public debt and tight financial conditions. India’s exposure to energy disruptions and limited participation in the AI boom demand policy agility.  Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize comes at a time of intensifying conflict and mounting challenges to the universality of human rights. Her choice for the Peace Nobel, notes our second editorial, delivers a restorative to the primacy of human rights in the global discourse, given that the South African jurist’s career has spanned the fight against apartheid, the prosecution of atrocities in Rwanda and efforts to advance gender justice and combat caste discrimination. Her work has also helped establish that rape and sexual assault could constitute acts of genocide. More recently, she chaired the UN commission that accused Israel of genocide in Gaza.  Nitin Desai argues that climate policy must shift beyond mitigation to prepare for unavoidable temperature rises, as countries’ emissions targets remain inadequate to meet the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C goal. With the threshold likely to be breached within years, India must integrate climate management into development planning, prioritising local adaptation to extreme heat, water stress and health risks. Desai proposes a National Climate Management Body bringing together the Centre, states and major cities to coordinate mitigation, resilience and compliance. He also calls for predictable climate finance, greater use of satellite imagery and AI, investment in carbon capture, and renewed international cooperation on technology and funding. India’s latest National Sample Survey reveals rising reported morbidity, continued dependence on private health care and stark disparities in treatment costs. The share of people reporting ailments nearly doubled in rural areas between 2017-18 and 2025, while private providers treated most non-hospitalised ailments, despite charging several times more than public facilities. Hospitalisation costs widen this financial burden, risking a medical poverty trap for vulnerable households. Vachaspati Shukla and Santosh Kumar Dash argue that expanding health insurance alone cannot ensure effective financial protection without accessible, reliable public facilities. They call for stronger primary care, district hospitals and service delivery so illness does not threaten household economic security. Neha Bhatt reviews Reetika Khera’s Freebies or Rights: Understanding Social Policy in India, which challenges the portrayal of welfare schemes as political hand-outs rather than fundamental rights. Drawing on field research and data, Khera examines programmes spanning food security, nutrition, healthcare and employment, questioning their funding, implementation and technological interventions. She warns that spending can serve corporate and philanthropic interests, while gaps in reliable data weaken accountability. Odisha, Tamil Nadu and Himachal Pradesh offer lessons in effective delivery, from nutrition and pensions to school meals and public canteens. The book makes a compelling case for treating social protection as a foundation of equality and opportunity.

entry.title: Best of Opinion: Disruption can't be stopped; resilience lies in response
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Specials / Best of Opinion: Disruption can't be stopped; resilience lies in responseBest of Opinion: Disruption can't be stopped; resilience lies in response

The real test of a system is not whether it can prevent every disruption. It is whether it has enough buffers, flexibility and institutional capacity

Reetesh Anand3 min read Last Updated : Oct 13 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTShocks are inevitable. Currencies come under pressure, economies are hit by unexpected disturbances, companies fail, financial vulnerabilities accumulate, and geopolitical orders fragment. The real test of a system is not whether it can prevent every disruption. It is whether it has enough buffers, flexibility and institutional capacity to absorb the blow without turning stress into breakdown. Our first editorial today, “Defending the rupee”, looks at India’s response to balance-of-payments pressure and a weakening currency. The RBI has several tools, including forex reserves and measures to influence liquidity and capital flows. These can reduce volatility and help prevent disorderly market movements. But they are ultimately shock absorbers, not substitutes for stronger fundamentals. Lasting external stability will depend on better export performance, more durable capital inflows and a current account that can withstand global turbulence.  The second editorial, “A Nobel for shocks”, takes the idea into macroeconomics. The Nobel-recognised work discussed in the editorial helped economists understand how unexpected disturbances travel through economies and why some shocks fade quickly while others produce prolonged effects. Frictions in labour, prices, finance and expectations can amplify disturbances, while policy can either cushion or worsen them. The lesson is not that economies can be made shock-proof, but that understanding transmission matters enormously when disruption arrives. M S Sahoo and Sanjeev Pandey’s column, “Maximising value, not the haircut”, applies the logic to insolvency. Corporate failure is itself a shock, but the IBC should not be judged only by the gap between creditors’ original claims and eventual recoveries. Once a company is distressed, much of its value may already have been destroyed. The more meaningful question is whether the resolution process preserves and maximises what remains, keeps viable assets productive and reallocates resources efficiently. The purpose of insolvency is not to pretend the loss never happened, but to prevent further destruction. Anoop Singh’s column, “Are financial risks now building?”, turns to the financial system as a whole. Stretched valuations, non-bank finance, fiscal pressures, technological change and geopolitical uncertainty can interact in ways that are difficult to predict. The challenge for policymakers is to identify vulnerabilities early, maintain adequate buffers and ensure risks do not migrate unnoticed across markets and institutions. Financial stability depends on resilience before the shock, not improvisation after it. “Middle powers’ unconvincing new statecraft”, Talmiz Ahmad’s review of Workarounding, edited by Maximilian Mayer, Gedaliah Afterman, Narayanappa Janardhan & Laura Mahrenbach, looks at geopolitics. As the international order becomes more fragmented, middle powers are experimenting with new coalitions and workarounds. But whether these arrangements can genuinely absorb geopolitical pressure or provide strategic room remains uncertain. Disruption cannot always be stopped, show these pieces. Resilience lies in what happens next.

entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Specials / Best of Opinion: Feedback ignored may return as friction, mistrust, failureBest of Opinion: Feedback ignored may return as friction, mistrust, failure

Healthy systems do not just impose, regulate or command. They also listen, learn and adjust before feedback becomes breakdown

Reetesh Anand New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 12 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTStrong systems do not just act but also listen. Tax authorities need to hear what compliance feels like for businesses. Election bodies need to respond to questions about credibility. Electricity markets need to absorb the signal sent by falling renewable costs. Infrastructure planning needs to respect what mountains and rivers are telling us. Democracies, too, weaken when competing sides stop hearing each other. The common lesson across all these issues is that feedback ignored eventually returns as friction, mistrust or failure. Our first editorial today, “From enforcement to trust”, looks at the GST regime after years of aggressive action against evasion and fraud. Enforcement was necessary, but the next stage cannot be built on permanent suspicion. Businesses need simpler procedures, predictable rules, fewer intrusive interventions and a system where compliant taxpayers are not treated as potential offenders by default. The editorial argues for a shift from enforcement-heavy administration towards trust-based compliance. Tax reform matures when the state learns from how the system actually works for those inside it.  The second editorial, “A democratic debate”, turns to the Election Commission of India. Questions about electoral processes should not automatically be treated as attacks on the institution. Credibility is strengthened when concerns are answered, data is disclosed and scrutiny is taken seriously. Democratic institutions do not protect themselves by closing off debate; they strengthen themselves by engaging with it. Ajay Shah’s column, “Consequences of cheap electricity”, looks at the signal sent by falling renewable-energy costs. If clean electricity becomes substantially cheaper, it can reshape industrial location, production costs and competitiveness. But India will benefit only if power markets, transmission, regulation and pricing allow firms to respond to that signal. Cheap power is not just an energy story. It could alter the economic geography of manufacturing, but only if the institutional machinery is flexible enough to let prices guide investment. Sunita Narain’s column, “Himalayan blunders and beyond”, deals with a more physical form of feedback. Repeated landslides, floods and ecological damage in the Himalayas are warnings about the consequences of construction that ignores hydrology, geology and carrying capacity. The problem is not that the mountains have failed to warn us. It is that development repeatedly proceeds as though those warnings could be negotiated away. Better planning requires treating ecological signals as hard constraints, not inconveniences. “When culture wars killed democracy”, Hugh Eakin’s review of Victor Sebestyen’s Weimar Germany, looks back at history. The Weimar Germany experience shows how democratic systems could unravel when political disagreement turns into cultural warfare and rival camps stop recognising each other as legitimate participants. Healthy systems do not just impose, regulate or command. They also listen, learn and adjust before feedback becomes breakdown.

After process reforms, GST needs road map to shed exclusions

premium

The broader unfinished agenda for GST’s full benefits to accrue to the economy is the inclusion of items such as petrol, diesel, electricity and natural gas that remain outside its ambit

Business Standard Editorial Comment4 min read Last Updated : Oct 11 2026 | 10:44 PM ISTWhen India rolled out goods and services tax (GST) on July 1, 2017, there was a concern that the bureaucracy grappled with — the uncertainty about the revenue trajectory and the need to compensate the states for any revenue shortfall in the first five years of the new tax. One source of revenue was proceeds of the GST compensation cess levied on items such as automobiles and tobacco. The other way to address the revenue risk was to have enough checks to prevent evasion. The tax system, thus, remained geared to ensure compliance, but at the expense of procedural simplicity. But officials’ worry about revenue collection and unmanageable compensation requirement did turn out to be true when the first Covid-19 wave hit India, and GST revenues plummeted in April 2020.  Monthly gross GST receipts of the central and state governments, which averaged ₹95,515 crore in 2018-19 and ₹96,605 crore in 2019-20, fell to ₹32,172 crore in April 2020. Consequently, the central government had to borrow ₹2.69 trillion from the market to compensate the states for their revenue shortfall. The full repayment of that in 2025-26 offered the GST Council an opportunity in September last year to review the tax slabs and rates, phase out the cess, and offer a consumption stimulus by lowering the indirect tax on a range of daily use as well as aspirational items, ranging from toothpaste and shampoo to consumer electronics and cars in the biggest overhaul of the system. Also, the number of slabs was brought down to broadly two, 5 and 18 per cent, from the earlier four—5, 12, 18 and 28 per cent with cess. That helped to boost consumption demand. Private final consumption expenditure expanded 7.1 per cent in the March quarter of 2025-26 as compared to 5.6 per cent at the same time a year earlier.  The next logical step for reform obviously was cutting red tape and making life simpler for businesses. The tech-enabled tax system, which captures a large amount of data from multiple sources, has made it possible for the authorities to spot sources of revenue leakage. The GST Council’s decisions last week — to drop the arrest provision, lower the penalty from ₹25,000 to ₹10,000, recall notices issued for amounts below ₹10,000 and not to issue such notices in future, offer credits for taxes paid on input services from November and on capital goods from April next year, and simplify the norms for GST registration and refunds — are a major structural overhaul of the tax system. The prosecution threshold is also being raised from ₹1 crore to  ₹5 crore. These measures mark the transformation from a framework designed to deal with tax evasion by a few to one that facilitates honest tax payers based on trust.  However, the task is not over. Two proposals, one meant to offer annual return filing and quarterly tax payments to consumer-facing businesses with sales up to ₹5 crore and a second proposal to further ease input tax credit availability, are sought to be implemented from April next year after another round of deliberation. The broader unfinished agenda for GST’s full benefits to accrue to the economy is the inclusion of items such as petrol, diesel, electricity and natural gas that remain outside its ambit. If the tax rates are indeed going to be reviewed only once a year from hereon, that should free up the Council’s bandwidth to discuss and lay out a road map for such excluded items so that efficiencies and competitiveness are enhanced across the value chain and GST truly becomes “good and simple”.   Topics : GST goods and service tax GST Council cgst GST Act BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment
